content: @Thomas Waring asked if I could refactor out Kripke frames out of Modal Logic, opening this to keep track of the discussion (https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/528#discussion_r3162302960).

thanks! roughly my thought is that the notion of "model for a logic" should be generalised in a similar vein to InferenceSystem, to which it will connect via Sound and Complete predicates. certain classes of models might be worth generalising too, eg Kripke models exist for intuitionistic logic. let me know if / when this is on your or anyone's radar, i'd be interested to discuss :-)

Ah, now I understand! Yes, it's on the radar, and I think this could be a good time to begin discussing it together if you like. :⁠-⁠)

It'd be nice to find common ground for at least modal logic, HML, and propositional logic.
(I'd focus on modal logic and propositional logic first, though, probably easier.)

great :) the main thing i'm unsure of is if this should wait for your classes like HasTensor — any sensible semantics for a logic should define the interpretation of a proposition inductively, and maybe we express this by (mutatis mutandis) Model.interp (HasAnd.and A B) = Model.and A B. my feeling is that this should be a condition on the model (something like Model.RespectsAnd) rather than being baked into the definition of a model, but again i'm not sure & i'm keen to to hear more about your plans re HasTensor / LawfulTensor etc

I think the two can proceed in parallel for now. My informal thought was to begin by specifying Tensor to give access to the tensor notation (but #CSLib > Notation for logical connectives might change this) and then LawfulTensor (parameterised over an InferenceSystem) to specify properties in terms of LogicalEquivalence.
i've put a proposal for a general typeclass for model of logic as a draft PR cslib#582 — interested to hear thoughts!
I left some comments in cslib#582.
@Thomas Waring re: Kripke models, this is one of the long term goals of HoTT lean and SynthLean. Although, I'm not sure how active the project still is.

thanks for the comments @Ching-Tsun Chou — updated PR at cslib#587 with different branch name
the idea with InterpModels is in the spirit of denotational semantics, the example i gave was Heyting semantics of propositional logic: given a model (a heyting algebra and a valuation of the atoms) each proposition has an interpretation as an element of the heyting algebra, and the model satisfies that proposition if its interpretation is the top element — in more generality there might be other "valid interpretations", hence the definition of a subset of Ground M to pick out such interpretations. the classes AlgebraicAnd are mostly there as an example of how common proof patterns might be generalised across different examples, for example, if filter M is an upper set, then AlgebraicAnd (in a semilattice) implies that ⊨[M] A ∧ B implies ⊨[M] A.

your concern with ParamModels is fair, i added a specific class because it's common to consider separately "local satisfaction" at a specific world w : Param M and "global satisfaction" at all world (this is the derived instance of Models from ParamModels). does anyone closer to modal logic (which is the example i had in mind) have thoughts?

thanks for the pointer @Bas Spitters — does have HoTT have its own version of Kripke semantics? or give it specific importance? my intention with this PR was mostly to give us a canonical way to spell a common concept in logic developments in the same way we have InferenceSystem, and eventually to give us a way to generalise common proof patterns.

in general i fully expect names and notation to change, this was just supposed to be a concrete example of how it might look. once we settle on a design the examples should go in their own PRs / files

It's a direct extension of the Kripke semantics you mention, it goes via (pre)sheaf semantics for toposes (HOL) to oo-toposes as models for type theory.
This shouldnt interfere with your PR, it's just context for the question you were asking about Kripke models.

See Kripke-Joyal forcing for type theory and uniform fibrations from some of the folks working on HoTTLean.

Also @Ching-Tsun Chou the PR got moved before I had a chance to comment, but in this context the verbiage "forcing" is standard.

thanks both, i haven't thought deeply about whether more categorical flavoured semantics could work with this formalism but (pre)sheaf semantics is something i am interested in (so far only in a non-lean way)
If you want a concrete application, iris lean should be based on the topos of trees, via Synth Lean, ... at least that's a research program we started a decade ago: https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.09263

May I suggest that before venturing into categorical logic and intuitionistic semantics, we first get good old classical logic going? I personally find it hard to follow the definitions if they are not illustrated on classical logic (including classical modal logic).

We already have some shallowly embedded temporal logic stuff in cslib:
https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/blob/main/Cslib/Foundations/Data/OmegaSequence/Temporal.lean
It would be nice if such things can be put into a proper framework.

I don't think it has to be an either/or situation. My own involvement in CSLib started because of categorical semantics, it's just not in the library yet because the universe issues are a pain. Plenty of space for people to work on whatever interests them.

I admit I am impatient in wanting some usable temporal logic in cslib. But it does seem to me that classical logic is the minimum requirement that any general definitions about fundamental concepts in logic (such as models and satisfaction relation) should support.

certainly i agree a general framework should support classical logic, at least for the propositional case boolean algebra semantics is a special case of the Heyting models i've defined as an example — i've put a rough idea of how classical semantics (in Prop) would be spelled at the end of the file. i can't comment in any depth on modal logic, but i did my best to faithfully recreate the notions from that part of the library also
Thanks for adding the InterpModels for classical logic in the PR. I left some comments in the PR.

Ching-Tsun Chou said:

I admit I am impatient in wanting some usable temporal logic in cslib. But it does seem to me that classical logic is the minimum requirement that any general definitions about fundamental concepts in logic (such as models and satisfaction relation) should support.

Can't we just extend one of the current HML or Modal Logic for that? Is it a matter of 'just doing it' or do we lack a clear recipe to achieve something?

@Ching-Tsun Chou regarding you last comments on cslib#587

  1. the canonical example of a model which doesn't take the form InterpModels is that of Kripke frames for intuitionistic or modal logic — there you define the forcing / entailment relation directly on propositions, rather than interpreting them into some ground set / algebra / whatever
  2. the example of ParamModels is in the Modal section — i had to bundle things a little differently but effectively it is exactly what already exists in the Logics/Modal directory. the (global) model is a choice of a type of worlds, a reachability relation and the forcing relation at ground type. the reason i made this generalisation from the plain Models class if that it's (to my understanding) important to talk simultaneously about satisfaction at a specific world, and universally quantified satisfaction in the whole model — for example, the general definitions i give for theory and logic respectively for Models and ParamModels instances match exactly the existing concepts with those names in the Modal directory. All of this is possible to state simply with Models and the sigma type, but i think it's a common enough paradigm to deserve it's own treatment.

Fabrizio Montesi said:

Can't we just extend one of the current HML or Modal Logic for that? Is it a matter of 'just doing it' or do we lack a clear recipe to achieve something?

Indeed we could do that and cslib#413 is working toward that. But I was commenting on cslib#587 and I thought that the purpose of cslib#587 is to provide a unified framework into which all the previous ad-hoc approaches can be subsumed.

Thomas Waring said:

  1. the canonical example of a model which doesn't take the form InterpModels is that of Kripke frames for intuitionistic or modal logic — there you define the forcing / entailment relation directly on propositions, rather than interpreting them into some ground set / algebra / whatever

If that's case, it seems to me that a top priority is to see how the existing ad-hoc definitions for HML and modal logics can be unified under this new framework. In particular, we should figure out whether the (classical) propositional logic can be factored out so that it is not repeated in both.

Also, I suspect the a "direct definition" approach would give rise to a certain algebra so that the former can be reformulated as an InterpModel after all.

  1. the example of ParamModels is in the Modal section.

Since we already have modal logics in cslib, could you work out the details of modal logic semantics in terms of ParamModels?

are you asking that i rewrite the modal logic files using this framework? because i have given an instance of ParamModels for the models defined in Logics/Modal/Basic, and shown that the general purpose definitions logic and theory agree with what is defined there. i haven't looked properly at HML yet but at first glance it will also give an instance of ParamModels, and the notion of theory defined there also matches what i've defined — i'll add that to the file this weekend.
i'm not sure i follow your idea to reinterpret the Kripke-type models as having an interpretation — possibly it's related to the standard construction of a, say, Heyting algebra given by subsets of the type of worlds? i'm still inclined to think we lose some expressivity if we force all the models we define to take a specific shape

OK, I see what you are doing now: in the Modal section, Model means Modal.Model and Satisfies means Modal.Satisfies defined in a different file, not the Models and Models.Satisfies defined earlier in the same file. This is very confusing. I think you should keep the Modal. prefix to alert the reader.

At this point I have to ask you: what is the ultimate goal you want to achieve with cslib#587?

Another thing is that I still think the bundled design of ParamModels is a mistake. The design in Modal/Basic.lean shows that an unbundled design works perfectly well. Furthermore, note that the notation for judgement in Modal/Basic.lean puts the model before the world and puts both on the LHS of the turnstile ⊨, exactly as I suggested earlier.

thanks again, i've put the prefix back & added the HML example as well.

the PR should not be merged, it's goal was to give a concrete suggestion for how a common framework for models could look (i've updated the docstring to emphasise this) and some examples to demonstrate. i fully expect things like names and notation to change, which is why i hadn't addressed your notation suggestions while we were still figuring out the shape these classes will take — i'm happy to change it if the confusion makes it harder to review, though.

if the unbundled design is strongly preferred i'm absolutely happy to go with it. i've added an implementation of the Modal concepts using the model type Modal.Model World Atom × World as an example — the same could be done for HML with model type LTS State Label × State. In this design the Modal.theory and HML.theory would be stated as the Models.logic of a singleton.

my reasoning for adding the bundled ParamModels was to match the concepts defined elsewhere, where entailment can be local or global — of course those concepts are not technically different, as you pointed out, so the question has more to do with whether we want to capture the conceptual different. to implement the HML and Modal examples, it would be enough to have Param as a parameter to the instance (ie of shape ParamModels (Modal.Proposition Atom) (Modal.Model World Atom) World), which i'd be more than happy with too, if that's preferred.

Thanks for the update! I think the unbundled modal Models looks pretty good. This is especially so because we don't even need a dependent type here. Is there an example where ParamModels.Param is a genuine dependent type?

There is another thing that bothers me: why did you choose to order the two arguments of Models in the way shown below, which is the opposite of the order in Satisfies and in the notation? Wouldn't it be better to use the same order (namely, (β : Type*) (α : outParam Type*)) everywhere? The same comment applies to ParamModels, HasInterp, and InterpModels as well.

class Models (α : outParam Type*) (β : Type*) where
  /-- `Satisfies b a` has the intended semantics "`a` is valid in the model `b`". -/
  Satisfies : β → α → Prop

scoped notation "⊨[" b "] " a => Models.Satisfies b a

Finally, I wonder if more suggestive names can be found for α and β. Maybe Formula and Model? I think such suggestive names will make it much easier to read the definitions, even if they may mislead in some cases.

okay i think i'm convinced that the representing satisfaction at a specific world by a product would be ergonomic enough to render ParamModels unnecessary — i've rewritten the file (left the old one up for comparison) in a new commit, and made the changes to notation and arguments you've suggested.
i'm interested in how this looks to people who worked on current Modal and HML developments, if any of @Fabrizio Montesi @Alexandre Rademaker or your collaborators whose zulip names i don't know have time to review :)

The current code looks much better and easier to read with the suggestive type names. My final suggestion is that the code depending on HasInterp be split out because it is for a specific style of semantics which probably not all logics will use.

great, thanks again for taking such a thorough look.
i think you're right about HasInterp — possibly it should even be moved out of the Logic namespace, in case there are applications to other kinds of semantics (eg interpreting types in a category, etc)
